newsitem.title: USA: Energy industry uneasy about potential Gore moves.
newsitem.headline: Energy industry uneasy about potential Gore moves.

text.p: Results in the U.S. presidential and Congressional races did little to change the outlook for energy policies in Congress next year, with the opening of electricity markets expected to dominate the agenda.

But energy industry officials were wary of Vice President Al Gore, an avowed environmentalist, rising to the fore in the Clinton administration's second term as he primes for the presidential race in 2000.
"Today begins the Gore campaign. Frankly I'm a little worried," said Peggy Welsh, executive director of the Electric Generation Association.

Environmental Protection Agency plans, opposed by refiners, to tighten air quality standards and expand use of clean reformulated gasoline could be reinforced by Gore, said Urvan Sternfels, president of the National Petroleum Refiners Association.
"There are several initiatives all focused on the same thing -- a very heightened environmental agenda," he said.
On the administration side, the big unknown remains who will replace Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary, who said Wednesday she was stepping down.
While she was under fire in Congress over the last year for her extensive travels overseas to promote U.S. business ventures, industry officials respected her more than her predecessors.
"We could do a lot worse as far as the industry is concerned," said Sternfels.

Rep. Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat, whose name has been circulating as a possible replacement, is knowledgable on energy issues, coming from a major natural gas producing state which also houses Energy Department research labs. He is also considered well-versed on electricity issues.
As for Congress, bipartisanship was the word for the day, with the Republicans having won a slimmer majority in the House.

Judging from the last three months of the 104th Congress, when the House and Senate worked out compromises with the White House, some industry officials predicted that Congress would steer away from sharp conflicts.

"We're hoping that we can continue in this positive mode of putting together realistic common sense changes that will get this industry moving again in the new year," said Denise Bode, president of the Independent Petroleum Association of America.
All the committee and subcommittee chairmen in the House and Senate who hold sway over energy, tax, environment and lands issues relevant to the energy industry remained in Congress.

The House is expected to be the prime mover on electric utility legislation as the expected Republican and Democrat leaders on the Senate Energy Commmittee, Sen. Frank Murkowski of Alaska and Sen. Dale Bumpers of Arkansas, are not as eager to force states to provide "customer choice" rapidly.
If the Republicans were chastened by their narrower majority in the House, it could bolster efforts to forge a consensus on the electricity issue, industry officials said.
"(Electricity) has always has been bipartisan issue," said Welsh. "Both sides are going to look for win-win on bipartisan stuff."

"A bipartisan bill (from the House) might be easier for the Senate to work with," said John Anderson, executive director of the Electricity Consumers Resource Council, which represents industrial consumers.
A change at the helm of the Energy Department could shift the direction the administration is moving in on electricity legislation.

The White House made clear in budget remarks this year that it favored competition in electricity markets. However, in contrast to proposals offered in Congress, Deputy Secretary Charles Curtis said recently he was leaning against forcing states to break local utility monopolies.
